## About Dataset

**About Dataset**  
 The World University Rankings 2023 dataset include 1,799 universities across 104 countries and regions, making them the largest and most diverse university rankings to date. The table is based on 13 carefully calibrated performance indicators that measure an institution’s performance across four areas: teaching, research, knowledge transfer and international outlook. This year’s ranking analyzed over 121 million citations across more than 15.5 million research publications and included survey responses from 40,000 scholars globally. Overall, we collected over 680,000 datapoints from more than 2,500 institutions that submitted data.  
**Features**  
 This dataset includes following 13 features:  
**1)**University Rank**2)**Name of University**3)**Location**4)**No of student**5)**No of student per staff**6)**International Student**7)**Female :Male Ratio**8)**OverAll Score**9)**Teaching Score**10)**Research Score**11)**Citations Score**12)**Industry Income Score**13)**International Outlook Score

**Atlanta**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-14) is the [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_capitals_in_the_United_States "List of capitals in the United States") and [most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Georgia_(U.S._state) "List of municipalities in Georgia (U.S. state)") of the U.S. state of [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"). It is the [county seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of [Fulton County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulton_County,_Georgia "Fulton County, Georgia") and extends into neighboring [DeKalb County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeKalb_County,_Georgia "DeKalb County, Georgia"). With a population of 498,715 at the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census") and an estimated 529,110 in 2025, Atlanta is the eighth-most populous city in the [Southeast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_United_States "Southeastern United States") and the [36th-most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_cities_by_population "List of United States cities by population") in the United States.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-15) Atlanta is classified as a [Beta+ global city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globalization_and_World_Cities_Research_Network#Beta_+ "Globalization and World Cities Research Network"). The [Atlanta metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Atlanta "Metro Atlanta") has an estimated population of over 6.4 million and is the [sixth-largest metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_metropolitan_statistical_areas "List of metropolitan statistical areas") in the United States.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-16) Situated among the foothills of the [Appalachian Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains "Appalachian Mountains") at an elevation of just over 1,000 feet (300 m) above sea level, Atlanta features a unique topography that includes rolling hills, lush greenery, and the [densest urban tree coverage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_tree_canopy "Atlanta tree canopy") of any major city in the United States.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-AIAGuide-17)

Atlanta was originally founded as the [terminus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_terminus "Rail terminus") of a major state-sponsored [railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railroad "Railroad"), but soon became the convergence point for several railroad lines, spurring its rapid growth. The largest of these was the [Western and Atlantic Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_and_Atlantic_Railroad "Western and Atlantic Railroad"), from which the name "Atlanta" is derived, reflecting the city's growing reputation as a major transportation hub.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-NGEAtlanta-18) During the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), the city served a strategically important role for [the Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Confederacy "The Confederacy"). It was captured in 1864 following the [Atlanta campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_campaign "Atlanta campaign"), and under Union General [William T. Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Tecumseh_Sherman "William Tecumseh Sherman"), Atlanta was almost entirely burned to the ground during the [March to the Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherman's_March_to_the_Sea "Sherman's March to the Sea").

Atlanta rebounded dramatically in the post–Civil War period and quickly became a national industrial center and the unofficial capital of the "[New South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South "New South")". After [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Atlanta emerged as a manufacturing and technology hub.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-jstor509-19) During the 1950s and 1960s, it became a major organizing center of the [American civil rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_civil_rights_movement "American civil rights movement"), with [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr."), [Ralph Abernathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Abernathy "Ralph Abernathy"), and many other locals serving as prominent leaders.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-20) In the modern era, Atlanta has remained a major transportation center, with [Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartsfield%E2%80%93Jackson_Atlanta_International_Airport "Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport") becoming the [world's busiest airport by passenger traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_airports_by_passenger_traffic "List of busiest airports by passenger traffic") in 1998. It has maintained this position every year since, except in 2020, with an estimated 93.7 million passengers in 2022.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-23)

With a [nominal gross domestic product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nominal_GDP "Nominal GDP") (GDP) of $473 billion in 2021, Atlanta has the 11th-largest economy among U.S. cities and the 22nd-largest in the world.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-24) Its economy is diverse, with dominant sectors including transportation, aerospace, logistics, healthcare, news and media operations, film and television production, information technology, finance, biomedical research, and public policy. Atlanta established itself on the world stage when it won the bid to host the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics"). The Games had a lasting impact on Atlanta's development into the 21st century, leading to significant investment in the city's universities, parks, and tourism industry.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-25) The [gentrification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentrification_of_Atlanta "Gentrification of Atlanta") of some of its neighborhoods has intensified in the 21st century with the growth of the [Atlanta Beltline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Beltline "Atlanta Beltline")[rail trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_trail "Rail trail"), altering Atlanta's [demographics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Atlanta "Demographics of Atlanta"), [politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Atlanta "Government of Atlanta"), [aesthetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture_of_Atlanta "Architecture of Atlanta"), and [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#Arts_and_culture).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-26)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-28)

## History

Main article: [History of Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Atlanta "History of Atlanta")

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Atlanta "Timeline of Atlanta").

### Native American settlements

For thousands of years prior to the arrival of European settlers in [North Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Georgia "North Georgia"), the indigenous [Creek people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscogee "Muscogee"), [Cherokee people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee "Cherokee"), and their ancestors inhabited the area.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-29)[Standing Peachtree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_Peachtree "Standing Peachtree"), a Creek village where [Peachtree Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peachtree_Creek "Peachtree Creek") flows into the [Chattahoochee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattahoochee_River "Chattahoochee River"), was the closest Native American settlement to what is now Atlanta.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-buckhead-30) Through the early 19th century, European Americans systematically encroached on the Creek of northern Georgia, forcing them out of the area from 1802 to 1825.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-31) The Creek were forced to leave the area in 1821, under [Indian Removal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_removal "Indian removal") by the federal government, and European American settlers arrived the following year.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-NGE_-_DeKalb_County-32)

### Western and Atlantic Railroad

In 1836, the [Georgia General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_General_Assembly "Georgia General Assembly") voted to build the [Western and Atlantic Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_and_Atlantic_Railroad "Western and Atlantic Railroad") in order to provide a link between the port of [Savannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannah,_Georgia "Savannah, Georgia") and the [Midwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwestern_United_States "Midwestern United States").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-W&ARR-33) The initial route was to run southward from [Chattanooga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattanooga,_Tennessee "Chattanooga, Tennessee") to a terminus east of the [Chattahoochee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattahoochee_River "Chattahoochee River"), which would be linked to Savannah. After engineers surveyed various possible locations for the terminus, the "[zero milepost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Zero_Mile_Post "Atlanta Zero Mile Post")" was driven into the ground in what is now Foundry Street, [Five Points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Points,_Atlanta "Five Points, Atlanta"). When asked in 1837 about the future of the little village, [Stephen Harriman Long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Harriman_Long "Stephen Harriman Long"), the railroad's chief engineer said the place would be good "for one tavern, a blacksmith shop, a grocery store, and nothing else".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-34) A year later, the area around the milepost had developed into a settlement, first known as _Terminus_, and later _Thrasherville_, after a local merchant who built homes and a [general store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_store "General store") in the area.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-ThrashervilleHistoricalMarker-35) By 1842, the town had six buildings and 30 residents and was renamed _[Marthasville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marthasville,\_Georgia "Marthasville, Georgia")_ to honor Governor [Wilson Lumpkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Lumpkin "Wilson Lumpkin")'s daughter Martha. Later, [John Edgar Thomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edgar_Thomson "John Edgar Thomson"), Chief Engineer of the [Georgia Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Railroad_and_Banking_Company "Georgia Railroad and Banking Company"), suggested the town be renamed _Atlanta_, supposedly a feminine version of the word "Atlantic", referring to the Western and Atlantic Railroad.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-NGEAtlanta-18) (Atalanta was also Martha Lumpkin's middle name.) The residents approved, and the town was incorporated as Atlanta on December 29, 1847.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-36)

### American Civil War

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Auction_and_negro_sales_1864.jpg/250px-Auction_and_negro_sales_1864.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Auction_and_negro_sales_1864.jpg)

[George N. Barnard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_N._Barnard "George N. Barnard")'s 1864 photograph of a [slave trader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slave_trader "Slave trader")'s business on Whitehall Street shows a corporal from the [United States Colored Troops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Colored_Troops "United States Colored Troops") sitting by the door.

By 1860, Atlanta's population had grown to 9,554.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-37)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-38) During the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), the nexus of multiple railroads in Atlanta made the city a strategic hub for the distribution of military supplies.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-39)

In 1864, the [Union Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Army "Union Army") moved southward following the capture of Chattanooga and began its [invasion of north Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_campaign "Atlanta campaign"). The region surrounding Atlanta was the location of several major army battles, culminating with the [Battle of Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Atlanta "Battle of Atlanta") and a four-month-long siege of the city by the Union Army under the command of General [William Tecumseh Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Tecumseh_Sherman "William Tecumseh Sherman"). On September 1, 1864, [Confederate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America "Confederate States of America") General [John Bell Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bell_Hood "John Bell Hood") decided to retreat from Atlanta, and he ordered the destruction of all public buildings and possible assets that could be of use to the Union Army. On the next day, Mayor [James Calhoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Calhoun_(politician,_born_1811) "James Calhoun (politician, born 1811)") surrendered Atlanta to the Union Army, and on September 7, Sherman ordered the city's civilian population to evacuate. On November 11, 1864, Sherman prepared for the Union Army's [March to the Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherman's_March_to_the_Sea "Sherman's March to the Sea") by ordering the destruction of Atlanta's remaining military assets.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-40)

### Reconstruction and late 19th century

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Marietta-Street-Atlanta.jpg/250px-Marietta-Street-Atlanta.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marietta-Street-Atlanta.jpg)

Marietta Street, 1864

After the Civil War ended in 1865, Atlanta was gradually rebuilt during the [Reconstruction era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_era "Reconstruction era"). The work attracted many new residents. Due to the city's superior [rail transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transportation "Rail transportation") network, the [state capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_historical_capitals "List of U.S. state historical capitals") was moved from [Milledgeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milledgeville,_Georgia "Milledgeville, Georgia") to Atlanta in 1868.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-41) In the 1880 Census, Atlanta had surpassed Savannah as Georgia's largest city.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-42)

Beginning in the 1880s, [Henry W. Grady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_W._Grady "Henry W. Grady"), the editor of the _[Atlanta Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta\_Constitution "Atlanta Constitution")_ newspaper, promoted Atlanta to potential investors as a city of the "[New South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South "New South")" that would be based upon a modern economy and less reliant on agriculture. By 1885, the founding of the Georgia School of Technology (now the [Georgia Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Georgia_Tech "History of Georgia Tech")) and the [Atlanta University Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_University_Center "Atlanta University Center"), a consortium of [historically black colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically_black_colleges "Historically black colleges") made up of units for men and women, had established Atlanta as a center for higher education. In 1895, Atlanta hosted the [Cotton States and International Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton_States_and_International_Exposition "Cotton States and International Exposition"), which attracted nearly 800,000 attendees and successfully promoted the New South's development to the world.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-43)

### 20th century

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Peachtree1907.jpg/250px-Peachtree1907.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Peachtree1907.jpg)

In 1907, Peachtree Street, the main street of Atlanta, was busy with streetcars and automobiles.

During the first decades of the 20th century, Atlanta enjoyed a period of unprecedented growth. In three decades' time, Atlanta's population tripled as the city limits expanded to include nearby streetcar suburbs. The city's skyline grew taller with the construction of the [Equitable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equitable_Building_(Atlanta_1892) "Equitable Building (Atlanta 1892)"), [Flatiron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flatiron_Building_(Atlanta) "Flatiron Building (Atlanta)"), [Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Mack_Robinson_College_of_Business_Administration_Building "J. Mack Robinson College of Business Administration Building"), and [Candler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candler_Building_(Atlanta) "Candler Building (Atlanta)") buildings. [Sweet Auburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_Auburn "Sweet Auburn") emerged as a center of Black commerce. The period was also marked by strife and tragedy. Increased racial tensions led to the [Atlanta Race Riot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Race_Riot "Atlanta Race Riot") of 1906, when Whites attacked Blacks, leaving at least 27 people dead and over 70 injured, with extensive damage in Black neighborhoods. In 1913, [Leo Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Frank "Leo Frank"), a Jewish-American factory superintendent, was convicted of the murder of a 13-year-old girl in a highly publicized trial. He was sentenced to death, but the governor commuted his sentence to life. An enraged and organized [lynch mob](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynching "Lynching") took him from jail in 1915 and hanged him in [Marietta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marietta,_Georgia "Marietta, Georgia"). The Jewish community in Atlanta and across the country were horrified.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-44)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-45) On May 21, 1917, the [Great Atlanta Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Atlanta_Fire_of_1917 "Great Atlanta Fire of 1917") destroyed 1,938 buildings in what is now the [Old Fourth Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Fourth_Ward "Old Fourth Ward"), resulting in one fatality and the displacement of 10,000 people.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-NGEAtlanta-18)

On December 15, 1939, Atlanta hosted the [premiere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiere "Premiere") of _[Gone with the Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gone\_with\_the\_Wind\_(film) "Gone with the Wind (film)")_, the epic film based on the best-selling novel by Atlanta's [Margaret Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Mitchell "Margaret Mitchell"). The gala event at [Loew's Grand Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loew's_Grand_Theatre "Loew's Grand Theatre") was attended by the film's legendary producer, [David O. Selznick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_O._Selznick "David O. Selznick"), and the film's stars [Clark Gable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Gable "Clark Gable"), [Vivien Leigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivien_Leigh "Vivien Leigh"), and [Olivia de Havilland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivia_de_Havilland "Olivia de Havilland"), but Oscar winner [Hattie McDaniel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hattie_McDaniel "Hattie McDaniel"), an African-American actress, was barred from the event due to racial segregation laws.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-46)

Atlanta played a vital role in the Allied effort during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). Colonel [Blake Van Leer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blake_Van_Leer "Blake Van Leer"), the president of Georgia Tech, played a significant part by lobbying war-related manufacturing companies like Lockheed Martin to move to Atlanta, successfully lobbying the Government to build military bases, in turn helping attract thousands of new residents through new jobs. Van Leer also launched major research centers, which included [Neely Nuclear Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neely_Nuclear_Research_Center "Neely Nuclear Research Center") and funds to help make Georgia Tech the "MIT" of the south while also founding [Southern Polytechnic State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Polytechnic_State_University "Southern Polytechnic State University").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-49)

These new defense industries attracted thousands of new residents and generated revenues, resulting in rapid population and economic growth. In the 1950s, the city's newly constructed highway system, supported by federal subsidies, allowed middle-class Atlantans the ability to relocate to the suburbs. As a result, the city began to make up an ever-smaller proportion of the metropolitan area's population.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-NGEAtlanta-18)

### Civil rights movement

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Martin_Luther_King_Jr_Coretta_Scott_King_Tomb.jpg/250px-Martin_Luther_King_Jr_Coretta_Scott_King_Tomb.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Martin_Luther_King_Jr_Coretta_Scott_King_Tomb.jpg)

The grave of Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King is within the [Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr._National_Historical_Park "Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park") in Atlanta proper.

[African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American") veterans returned from World War II seeking full rights in their country and began heightened activism. In exchange for support by that portion of the Black community that could vote, in 1948 the mayor ordered the hiring of the first eight African-American police officers in the city.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-50)

Much controversy preceded the [1956 Sugar Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_Sugar_Bowl "1956 Sugar Bowl"), when the [Pitt Panthers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_Pittsburgh_Panthers_football_team "1955 Pittsburgh Panthers football team"), with African-American fullback [Bobby Grier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Grier_(American_football_player) "Bobby Grier (American football player)") on the roster, met the [Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_Georgia_Tech_Yellow_Jackets_football_team "1955 Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets football team").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-fcflu-51) There had been controversy over whether Grier should be allowed to play due to his race, and whether Georgia Tech should even play at all due to Georgia's [Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Georgia "List of governors of Georgia")[Marvin Griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvin_Griffin "Marvin Griffin")'s opposition to racial integration.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-Mul%C3%A9-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-53)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-54) After Griffin publicly sent a telegram to the state's Board of Regents requesting Georgia Tech not to engage in racially integrated events, Georgia Tech's president [Blake R. Van Leer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blake_R._Van_Leer "Blake R. Van Leer") rejected the request and threatened to resign. Later, students from both Georgia Tech and the University of Georgia held a protest against Griffin's stance, which soon turned into a riot. The students broke windows, upturned parking meters, hung Griffin in effigy, and marched all the way to the governor's mansion, surrounding it until 3:30 a.m. Griffin publicly blamed Georgia Tech's president for the "riots" and requested he be replaced and Georgia Tech's state funding be cut off. On December 5 the Georgia Tech board of regents voted 13–1 in favor of allowing the game to proceed as scheduled.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-55)

In the 1960s, Atlanta became a major organizing center of the [civil rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement "Civil rights movement"), with [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr."), [Ralph Abernathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Abernathy "Ralph Abernathy"), and students from Atlanta's [historically black colleges and universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically_black_colleges_and_universities "Historically black colleges and universities") playing major roles in the movement's leadership. While Atlanta in the postwar years had relatively minimal racial strife compared to other cities, Blacks were limited by discrimination, segregation, and continued [disenfranchisement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disfranchisement_after_Reconstruction_era "Disfranchisement after Reconstruction era") of most voters.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-kruse-56) In 1961, the city attempted to thwart [blockbusting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockbusting "Blockbusting") by realtors by erecting road barriers in [Cascade Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascade_Heights "Cascade Heights"), countering the efforts of civic and business leaders to foster Atlanta as the "city too busy to hate."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-kruse-56)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-57)

Desegregation of the public sphere came in stages, with public transportation desegregated by 1959,[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-NGEbusDesegregation-58) the restaurant at [Rich's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rich's_(department_store) "Rich's (department store)") department store by 1961,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-59) movie theaters by 1963,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-60) and public schools by 1973 (nearly 20 years after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that segregated public schools were unconstitutional).[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-61)

In 1960, Whites comprised 61.7% of the city's population.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-census1-62) During the 1950s–70s, suburbanization and [White flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_flight "White flight") from urban areas led to a significant demographic shift.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-kruse-56) By 1970, African Americans were the majority of the city's population and exercised their recently enforced voting rights and political influence by electing Atlanta's first Black mayor, [Maynard Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maynard_Jackson "Maynard Jackson"), in 1973. Under Mayor Jackson's tenure, Atlanta's airport was modernized, strengthening the city's role as a transportation center. The opening of the [Georgia World Congress Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_World_Congress_Center "Georgia World Congress Center") in 1976 further confirmed Atlanta's rise as a convention city.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-GWCCfacts-63) Construction of the city's [subway system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Atlanta_Rapid_Transit_Authority "Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority") began in 1975, with rail service commencing in 1979.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-hist1970-64) Despite these improvements, Atlanta lost more than 100,000 residents between 1970 and 1990, over 20% of its population.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-nytimes1-65) At the same time, it developed new office space after attracting numerous corporations, with an increasing portion of workers from northern areas.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-66)

### 1996 Summer Olympic games

[![Image 28: A white flag with five differently colored interlocking rings in the center is seen atop a flagpole, against the backdrop of a stadium filled with spectators.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/JO_Atlanta_1996_-_Drapeau.jpg/250px-JO_Atlanta_1996_-_Drapeau.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JO_Atlanta_1996_-_Drapeau.jpg)

The Olympic flag waves at the 1996 Summer Olympic games.

Atlanta was selected as the site for the [1996 Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympic_Games "1996 Summer Olympic Games"). Following the [announcement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bids_for_the_1996_Summer_Olympics "Bids for the 1996 Summer Olympics"), the city government undertook several major construction projects to improve Atlanta's parks, sporting venues, and transportation infrastructure; however, for the first time, none of the $1.7 billion cost of the games was governmentally funded. While the games experienced transportation and accommodation problems and the [Centennial Olympic Park bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centennial_Olympic_Park_bombing "Centennial Olympic Park bombing") occurred despite extra security precautions,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-67) the spectacle was still a watershed event in Atlanta's history. According to former Mayor [Kasim Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasim_Reed "Kasim Reed"), the Olympic Games generated "a direct economic impact of at least USD 5 billion".[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-68)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-69) For the first time in Olympic history, every one of the record 197 national Olympic committees invited to compete sent athletes, sending more than 10,000 contestants participating in a record 271 events. The related projects, such as [Atlanta's Olympic Legacy Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta's_Olympic_Legacy_Program "Atlanta's Olympic Legacy Program") and civic efforts, initiated a fundamental transformation of the city in the following decade.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-nytimes1-65)

### 21st century

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/DARLINGTON_ATLANTA_DAY_SKYLINE_1.jpg/250px-DARLINGTON_ATLANTA_DAY_SKYLINE_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DARLINGTON_ATLANTA_DAY_SKYLINE_1.jpg)

Midtown has been a major growing center of the city since the turn of the 21st century.

During the 2000s, the city of Atlanta underwent a profound physical, [cultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_culture "Human culture"), and [demographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics "Demographics") change. As some of the African-American middle and upper classes also began to move to the suburbs, a booming economy drew numerous new migrants from other cities in the United States, who contributed to changes in the city's demographics. African Americans made up a decreasing portion of the population, from a high of 67% in 1990 to 54% in 2010.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-spelman-70) From 2000 to 2010, Atlanta gained 22,763 white residents, 5,142 Asian residents, and 3,095 Hispanic residents, while the city's Black population decreased by 31,678.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-blogs.ajc.com-71)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-nyt-031106-72) Much of the city's demographic change during the decade was driven by young, college-educated professionals: from 2000 to 2009, the [three-mile radius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intown_Atlanta "Intown Atlanta") surrounding [Downtown Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Atlanta "Downtown Atlanta") gained 9,722 residents aged 25 to 34 and holding at least a four-year degree, an increase of 61%.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-73) This was similar to the tendency in other cities for young, college educated, single or married couples to live in downtown areas.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-74)

In the lead-up to the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics"), the [Atlanta Housing Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Housing_Authority "Atlanta Housing Authority") demolished nearly all of its public housing.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-oakley-75)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-76)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-77) Residents instead received vouchers to pay for private housing; a wave of mixed housing was built using funding from the [HOPE VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HOPE_VI "HOPE VI") program under CEO Renee Lewis Glover (1994–2013).[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-trubey-78)

In 2005, the city approved the $2.8 billion [Beltline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Beltline "Atlanta Beltline") project. It was intended to convert a disused 22-mile freight railroad loop that surrounds the central city into an art-filled multi-use trail and light rail transit line, which would increase the city's park space by 40%.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-BeltlineFacts-79) The project stimulated retail and residential development along the loop, but has been criticized for its adverse effects on some Black communities.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-80) In 2013, the project received a federal grant of $18 million to develop the southwest corridor. In September 2019, the James M. Cox Foundation gave $6 million to the PATH Foundation which will connect the [Silver Comet Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Comet_Trail "Silver Comet Trail") to The Atlanta Beltline, which was expected to be completed by 2022. Upon completion, the total combined interconnected trail distance around Atlanta for the Atlanta Beltline and Silver Comet Trail will be the longest paved trail surface in the U.S., totaling about 300 miles (480 km).[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-BeltlineFacts-79)

Atlanta's cultural offerings expanded during the 2000s: the [High Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Museum_of_Art "High Museum of Art") doubled in size; the [Alliance Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_Theatre "Alliance Theatre") won a [Tony Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Award "Tony Award"); and art galleries were established on the once-industrial [Westside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midtown "West Midtown").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-online.wsj.com-81) The [College Football Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Football_Hall_of_Fame "College Football Hall of Fame") relocated to Atlanta and the [National Center for Civil and Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Center_for_Civil_and_Human_Rights "National Center for Civil and Human Rights") museum was constructed. The city of Atlanta was the subject of a [massive cyberattack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Atlanta_cyberattack "2018 Atlanta cyberattack") which began in March 2018.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-82) In December 2019, Atlanta hosted the [Miss Universe 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Universe_2019 "Miss Universe 2019") pageant competition.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-83)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-84)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-85) Atlanta was one of the host cities for the [2026 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_FIFA_World_Cup "2026 FIFA World Cup").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-86)

## Geography

Main article: [Geography of Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Atlanta "Geography of Atlanta")

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Atlanta_by_Sentinel-2_2022-04-19.jpg/250px-Atlanta_by_Sentinel-2_2022-04-19.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atlanta_by_Sentinel-2_2022-04-19.jpg)

Atlanta and its surrounding suburbs, from Sentinel-2A satellite, 2022

Atlanta encompasses 134.0 square miles (347.1 km 2), of which 133.2 square miles (344.9 km 2) is land and 0.85 square miles (2.2 km 2) is water.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-Census_2010-87) The city is situated in the [Deep South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_South "Deep South") of the [southeastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_United_States "Southeastern United States") among the foothills of the [Appalachian Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains "Appalachian Mountains"). At 1,050 feet (320 m) above mean sea level, Atlanta has the highest elevation among major cities east of the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-88) Atlanta straddles the [Eastern Continental Divide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Continental_Divide "Eastern Continental Divide"). Rainwater that falls on the south and east side of the divide flows into the Atlantic Ocean, while rainwater on the north and west side of the divide flows into the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-divide-89) Atlanta developed on a [ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridge "Ridge") south of the [Chattahoochee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattahoochee_River "Chattahoochee River"), which is part of the [ACF River Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACF_River_Basin "ACF River Basin"). The river borders the far northwestern edge of the city, and much of its natural habitat has been preserved, in part by the [Chattahoochee River National Recreation Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattahoochee_River_National_Recreation_Area "Chattahoochee River National Recreation Area").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-90)

Atlanta is 21 miles (34 km) southeast of [Marietta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marietta,_Georgia "Marietta, Georgia"),[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-91)27 miles (43 km) southwest of [Alpharetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpharetta,_Georgia "Alpharetta, Georgia"), 146 miles (235 km) southwest of [Greenville, South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenville,_South_Carolina "Greenville, South Carolina"),[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-92)147 miles (237 km) east of [Birmingham, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama"),[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-93) and 245 miles (394 km) southwest of [Charlotte, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte,_North_Carolina "Charlotte, North Carolina").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-94)

Despite having lost significant tree canopy coverage between 1973 and 1999, Atlanta now has the [densest urban tree coverage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_tree_canopy "Atlanta tree canopy") of any major city in the United States and is often called "City of Trees" or "The City in a Forest".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-AIAGuide-17)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-95)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-96)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-97)

#### Neighborhoods

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/AATL202503-0850_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-AATL202503-0850_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AATL202503-0850_(cropped).jpg)

Downtown Atlanta skyline

Atlanta is divided into 242 officially defined [neighborhoods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhoods_of_Atlanta "Neighborhoods of Atlanta").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-Atlanta_Neighborhoods-98) The city contains three major high-rise districts, which form a north–south axis along [Peachtree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peachtree_Street "Peachtree Street"): [Downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Atlanta "Downtown Atlanta"), [Midtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midtown_Atlanta "Midtown Atlanta"), and [Buckhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckhead "Buckhead").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-99) Surrounding these high-density districts are leafy, low-density neighborhoods, most of which are dominated by single-family homes.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-100)

[Downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Atlanta "Downtown Atlanta") contains the most office space in the metro area, much of it occupied by government entities. Downtown is home to the city's sporting venues and many of its tourist attractions.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-101)[Midtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midtown_Atlanta "Midtown Atlanta") is the city's second-largest business district, containing the offices of many of the region's law firms. Midtown is known for its art institutions, cultural attractions, institutions of higher education, and dense form.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-102)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-103)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-105)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-106)[Buckhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckhead "Buckhead"), the city's uptown district, is eight miles (13 km) north of Downtown and the city's third-largest business district. The district is marked by an urbanized core along [Peachtree Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peachtree_Street "Peachtree Street"), surrounded by suburban single-family neighborhoods situated among woods and rolling hills.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-nytimes2003-107)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-108)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-109)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-110)

[![Image 35](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Beath_Dickey_House_Exterior_2018.jpg/250px-Beath_Dickey_House_Exterior_2018.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Beath_Dickey_House_Exterior_2018.jpg)

[Beath-Dickey House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beath-Dickey_House "Beath-Dickey House") (1890) in [Inman Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inman_Park "Inman Park") neighborhood, 2018

Surrounding Atlanta's three high-rise districts are the city's low- and medium-density [neighborhoods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhoods_of_Atlanta "Neighborhoods of Atlanta"),[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-nytimes2003-107) where the [craftsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Craftsman "American Craftsman")[bungalow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bungalow "Bungalow") single-family home is dominant.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-111) The [eastside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastside_(Atlanta) "Eastside (Atlanta)") is marked by historic [streetcar suburbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streetcar_suburbs "Streetcar suburbs"), built from the 1890s to the 1930s as havens for the upper middle class. These neighborhoods, many of which contain their own villages encircled by shaded, architecturally distinct residential streets, include the [Victorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_architecture "Victorian architecture")[Inman Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inman_Park "Inman Park"), [Bohemian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemianism "Bohemianism")[East Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Atlanta "East Atlanta"), and eclectic [Old Fourth Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Fourth_Ward "Old Fourth Ward").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-Gournay-112)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-113) On the [westside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midtown "West Midtown") and along the [Beltline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Beltline "Atlanta Beltline") on the [eastside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastside,_Atlanta "Eastside, Atlanta"), former warehouses and factories have been converted into housing, retail space, and art galleries, transforming the once-industrial areas such as [West Midtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midtown "West Midtown") into model neighborhoods for [smart growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_growth "Smart growth"), historic rehabilitation, and infill construction.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-114)

In southwest Atlanta, neighborhoods closer to downtown originated as streetcar suburbs, including the historic [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_(Atlanta) "West End (Atlanta)"), while those farther from downtown retain a postwar suburban layout. These include [Collier Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collier_Heights "Collier Heights") and [Cascade Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascade_Heights "Cascade Heights"), historically home to most of the city's [upper middle-class African-American population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American_middle_class "African-American middle class").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-115)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-116)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-117) Northwest Atlanta contains the areas of the city to west of Marietta Boulevard and to the north of Martin Luther King Jr. Drive, including those neighborhoods remote to downtown, such as Riverside, Bolton and Whittier Mill. The latter is one of Atlanta's designated Landmark Historical Neighborhoods. Vine City, though technically Northwest, adjoins the city's Downtown area and has recently been the target of community outreach programs and economic development initiatives.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-118)

Gentrification of the city's neighborhoods is one of the more controversial and transformative forces shaping contemporary Atlanta. The [gentrification of Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentrification_of_Atlanta "Gentrification of Atlanta") has its origins in the 1970s, after many of Atlanta's neighborhoods had declined and suffered the urban decay that affected other major American cities in the mid-20th century. When neighborhood opposition successfully prevented two [freeways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_485_(Georgia) "Interstate 485 (Georgia)") from being built through the city's east side in 1975, the area became the starting point for Atlanta's [gentrification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentrification "Gentrification"). After Atlanta was awarded the Olympic Games in 1990, gentrification expanded into other parts of the city, stimulated by infrastructure improvements undertaken in preparation for the games. New development post-2000 has been aided by the [Atlanta Housing Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Housing_Authority "Atlanta Housing Authority")'s eradication of the city's public housing. As noted above, it allowed the development of these sites for mixed-income housing, requiring developers to reserve a considerable portion for affordable housing units. It has also provided for other former residents to be given vouchers to gain housing in other areas.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-husock-119) Construction of the Beltline has stimulated new and related development along its path.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-120)

#### Architecture

Main article: [Architecture of Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture_of_Atlanta "Architecture of Atlanta")

Most of Atlanta was burned in the final months of the American Civil War, depleting the city of a large stock of its historic architecture. Yet architecturally, the city had never been traditionally "southern": Atlanta originated as a railroad town rather than a southern seaport dominated by the planter class, such as [Savannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannah,_Georgia "Savannah, Georgia") or [Charleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_South_Carolina "Charleston, South Carolina"). Because of its later development, many of the city's landmarks share architectural characteristics with buildings in the Northeast or Midwest, as they were designed at a time of shared national architectural styles.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-Gournay-112)

[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Atlanta_Skyline_-_Piedmont_Park.png/250px-Atlanta_Skyline_-_Piedmont_Park.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atlanta_Skyline_-_Piedmont_Park.png)

The skyline of Midtown (viewed from [Piedmont Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piedmont_Park "Piedmont Park")) emerged with the construction of modernist [Colony Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_Square "Colony Square") in 1972.

During the late 20th century, Atlanta embraced the global trend of [modern architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_architecture "Modern architecture"), especially for commercial and institutional structures. Examples include the [State of Georgia Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Georgia_Building "State of Georgia Building"), built in 1966, and the [Georgia-Pacific Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia-Pacific_Tower "Georgia-Pacific Tower") in 1982. Many of the most notable examples from this period were designed by world-renowned Atlanta architect [John Portman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Portman_Jr. "John C. Portman Jr."). Most of the buildings that define the downtown skyline were designed by Portman during this period, including the [Westin Peachtree Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westin_Peachtree_Plaza "Westin Peachtree Plaza") and the [Atlanta Marriott Marquis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Marriott_Marquis "Atlanta Marriott Marquis"). In the latter half of the 1980s, Atlanta became one of the early homes of postmodern buildings that reintroduced classical elements to their designs. Many of Atlanta's tallest skyscrapers were built in this period and style, displaying tapering spires or otherwise ornamented crowns, such as [One Atlantic Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Atlantic_Center "One Atlantic Center") (1987), [191 Peachtree Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/191_Peachtree_Tower "191 Peachtree Tower") (1991), and the [Four Seasons Hotel Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Seasons_Hotel_Atlanta "Four Seasons Hotel Atlanta") (1992). Also completed during the era was the [Bank of America Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_America_Plaza_(Atlanta) "Bank of America Plaza (Atlanta)"), built in 1992. At 1,023 feet (312 m), it is the tallest building in the city and the 14th-tallest in the United States.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-121)

The city's embrace of modern architecture has often translated into an ambivalent approach toward historic preservation, leading to the destruction of many notable architectural landmarks. These include the [Equitable Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equitable_Building_(Atlanta_1892) "Equitable Building (Atlanta 1892)") (1892–1971), [Terminal Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_Station_(Atlanta) "Terminal Station (Atlanta)") (1905–1972), and the [Carnegie Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Library_(Atlanta) "Carnegie Library (Atlanta)") (1902–1977).[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-Guardian_preservation-122) In the mid-1970s, the [Fox Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Theatre_(Atlanta,_Georgia) "Fox Theatre (Atlanta, Georgia)"), now a cultural icon of the city, would have met the same fate if not for a grassroots effort to save it.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-Gournay-112) More recently, preservationists may have made some inroads. For example, in 2016 activists convinced the Atlanta City Council not to demolish the Atlanta-Fulton Central Library, the last building designed by noted architect [Marcel Breuer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Breuer "Marcel Breuer").[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-Central_Library_Saved-123)

### Climate

[![Image 37](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Atlanta_Skyline_-_enilykS_atnaltA.jpg/250px-Atlanta_Skyline_-_enilykS_atnaltA.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atlanta_Skyline_-_enilykS_atnaltA.jpg)

[![Image 38](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Georgia_snow_IMG_5076_%2824082748877%29.jpg/250px-Georgia_snow_IMG_5076_%2824082748877%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Georgia_snow_IMG_5076_(24082748877).jpg)

[Fall foliage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autumn_leaf_color "Autumn leaf color") and an early-winter snowfall in [Piedmont Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piedmont_Park "Piedmont Park")

Under the [Köppen classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"), Atlanta has a [humid subtropical climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate "Humid subtropical climate") (_Cfa_)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-124) with generous precipitation year-round, typical for the [Upland South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upland_South "Upland South"). The city is situated in [USDA Plant Hardiness Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardiness_zone "Hardiness zone") 8a, with the northern and western suburbs, as well as part of Midtown transitioning to 7b.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-125) Summers are hot and humid, with temperatures somewhat moderated by the city's elevation. Winters are overall mild but variable, occasionally susceptible to [snowstorms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_storm "Winter storm") even if in small quantities on several occasions, unlike the central and southern portions of the state.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-126)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-127) Warm air from the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico") can bring spring-like highs while strong Arctic air masses can push lows into the teens°F (−7 to −12°C).

July averages 80.9°F (27.2°C), with high temperatures reaching 90°F (32°C) on an average of 47 days per year, though 100°F (38°C) readings are not seen most years.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-NCDC_txt_KATL-128) January averages 44.8°F (7.1°C), with temperatures in the suburbs slightly cooler due largely to the [urban heat island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_heat_island "Urban heat island") effect. Lows at or below freezing can be expected 36 nights annually,[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-NOWData_NWS_Peachtree_City,_GA_(FFC)_-_ATLthr-129) but the last occurrences of temperatures below 10°F (−12°C) were [December 24, 2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/December_2022_North_American_winter_storm "December 2022 North American winter storm"),[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-NOWData_NWS_Peachtree_City,_GA_(FFC)_-_ATLthr-129) and [January 2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_2014_North_American_cold_wave "Early 2014 North American cold wave"), eight years apart. Extremes range from −9°F (−23°C) on [February 13, 1899](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Blizzard_of_1899 "Great Blizzard of 1899") to 106°F (41°C) on [June 30, 2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_2012_North_American_heat_wave "Summer 2012 North American heat wave").[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-NOWData_NWS_Peachtree_City,_GA_(FFC)_-_ATLthr-129) Average dewpoints in the summer range from 63.7°F (17.6°C) in June to 67.8°F (19.9°C) in July.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-noaasun-130)

Typical of the southeastern U.S., Atlanta receives abundant rainfall that is evenly distributed throughout the year, though late spring and early fall are somewhat drier. The average annual precipitation is 50.43 in (1,281 mm), while snowfall is typically light and rare, with a normal of 2.2 inches (5.6 cm) per winter.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-NOWData_NWS_Peachtree_City,_GA_(FFC)_-_ATLthr-129) The heaviest single snowfall occurred on January 23, 1940, with around 10 inches (25 cm) of snow.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-131) However, [ice storms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_storm "Ice storm") usually cause more problems than snowfall does, the most severe occurring on January 7, 1973.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-132) Tornadoes are rare in the city itself, but the [March 14, 2008, EF2 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Atlanta_tornado_outbreak "2008 Atlanta tornado outbreak") damaged prominent structures in downtown Atlanta.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-133)

The [2020 United States census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census") reported that Atlanta had a population of 498,715. The [population density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density "Population density") was 3,685.45 persons per [square mile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_mile "Square mile") (1,422.95/[km 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_kilometer "Square kilometer")). The racial and ethnic makeup of Atlanta (including Hispanics) was 51.0% Black or African American, 40.9% non-Hispanic white, 4.2% Asian, and 0.3% Native American, and 1.0% from other races. 2.4% of the population reported [two or more races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiracial_Americans "Multiracial Americans").[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-157) Hispanics and Latinos of any race made up 6.0% of the city's population.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-AtlCensus-158) The median income for a household in the city was $77,655 in 2022.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-census.gov-159) The per capita income for the city was $60,778 in 2022.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-census.gov-159) Approximately 17.7% percent of the population was living below the [poverty line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_threshold "Poverty threshold") in 2022.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-census.gov-159) Circa 2024, of the Atlanta residents, 391,711 of them lived in Fulton County and 28,292 of them lived in DeKalb County.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-160)

Map of racial distribution in Atlanta, 2010 U.S. census. Each dot is 25 people: ⬤White⬤Black⬤Asian⬤Hispanic⬤Other

In the 1920s, the Black population began to grow in Southern metropolitan cities like Atlanta, [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham,_Alabama "Birmingham, Alabama"), [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston"), and [Memphis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee").[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-161) Since the 1970s, Atlanta has been widely recognized as a hub of African American political activism, education, entrepreneurship, and culture—earning it the reputation of being a [Black mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_mecca "Black mecca").[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-162)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-163)[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-164) However, in the 1990s, Atlanta started to experience [Black flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_flight "Black flight").[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-165)[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-166) African Americans have moved outside the city seeking a lower cost of living or better public schools. The African American share of Atlanta's population has declined faster than any other racial group.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-11Alive.com-2021-167) The city's share of Black residents shrank from 67% in 1990 to 47% in 2020. Blacks made up nine percent of new Atlanta residents between 2010 and 2020.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-11Alive.com-2021-167)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-spelman-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-blogs.ajc.com-71) At the same time, Atlanta is home to a sizable foreign-born Black population,[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-168) notably from [Eritrea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eritrea "Eritrea"), [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia"), [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana "Ghana"), [Somalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somalia "Somalia"), [Liberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberia "Liberia"), and [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria").[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-169)

With many notable investments occurring in Atlanta initiated by the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics"), the non-Hispanic White population of Atlanta began to rebound after several decades of [White flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_flight "White flight") to Atlanta's suburbs.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-170)[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-171) Between 2000 and 2020, the proportion of Whites in the city had strong growth. In two decades, Atlanta's White population grew from 33% to 39% of the city's population. Whites made up the majority of new Atlanta residents between 2010 and 2020.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-11Alive.com-2021-167)[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-172)

The Hispanic and Latino populations in Metro Atlanta have experienced significant growth.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-173) The largest Hispanic ancestries in Atlanta are [Mexican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_Americans "Mexican Americans"), [Puerto Rican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stateside_Puerto_Ricans "Stateside Puerto Ricans") and [Cuban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Americans "Cuban Americans").[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-174) There is a growing population of Mexican ancestry throughout the region, with notable concentrations along the Buford Highway and I-85 corridor, and now extending into Gwinnett County.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta#cite_note-175) In 2013, Metro Atlanta had the
